lesson.title: The Company Town Revolts: The Pullman Strike of 1894
lesson.summary: When George Pullman cut wages but not rents in his model company town outside Chicago, a nationwide railroad boycott led by Eugene V. Debs paralyzed rail traffic until federal troops and a court injunction broke the strike.
lesson.body:
George Pullman's company built the luxurious sleeping cars that rode the nation's rapidly expanding rail network, described in the story of Railroad Expansion, and Pullman housed many of his workers in a company town he built just south of Chicago, where the company owned the housing, ran the stores, and deducted rent directly from workers' paychecks.

When the depression that followed the Panic of 1893 hit the company, Pullman cut wages by roughly a quarter, but did not lower the rents or store prices he charged workers in the company town, leaving many employees with take home pay barely enough to survive. Workers who tried to petition Pullman for relief were rebuffed, and some were fired.

Many Pullman workers belonged to the American Railway Union, led by Eugene V. Debs. Unlike the AFL's craft based approach of organizing workers trade by trade, the American Railway Union was an industrial union that organized all railroad workers together regardless of their specific job. When Pullman refused to negotiate, the union voted to boycott any train that included a Pullman car, and the boycott spread rapidly, effectively paralyzing much of the nation's rail traffic by the summer of 1894.

Railroad owners, organized as the General Managers' Association, deliberately attached Pullman cars to trains carrying U.S. mail, giving the federal government grounds to intervene. U.S. Attorney General Richard Olney, himself a former railroad lawyer, obtained a sweeping federal injunction against the strike, and President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops into Chicago in July 1894 over the strong objections of Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld, citing interference with the mail and interstate commerce. Violence followed, and dozens of people were killed in the resulting clashes.

The strike collapsed, and Debs was jailed for defying the federal injunction, a punishment the Supreme Court upheld in the 1895 case In re Debs. While in prison, Debs read socialist literature and emerged committed to socialism, later running for president several times as the Socialist Party's candidate. The Pullman Strike, like Homestead before it, demonstrated the federal government's willingness to side with employers against organized labor, and showed that even a broad industrial union could be broken when companies, courts, and the government acted together.
